<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Simulations were performed to investigate neutron-induced radioactivity in the iron (Fe) target and surrounding coolants (sodium-potassium alloy (NaK), lead (Pb), water (H
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O), liquid sodium (Na), and carbon dioxide (CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    )) by bombarding the target with 400 MeV carbon ions. Radionuclides produced within the target material and each coolant were evaluated over time using the FLUKA Monte Carlo code. The temporal evolution of all induced radionuclides was analyzed and visualized through time-dependent activity curves. Neutron yield was quantified at an incident energy of 400 MeV. It was observed that low-energy neutrons were the main cause of activation. During the shutdown of the accelerator,
                    <jats:sup>56</jats:sup>
                    Mn was observed with a high ratio inside the iron target, while
                    <jats:sup>41</jats:sup>
                    Ar,
                    <jats:sup>200</jats:sup>
                    Pb,
                    <jats:sup>11</jats:sup>
                    C, and
                    <jats:sup>24</jats:sup>
                    Na were identified as the primary contributors in the respective coolants: NaK, Lead, water, and liquid sodium. Specifically,
                    <jats:sup>11</jats:sup>
                    C was dominant in both water and CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    . From the start of irradiation to saturation, and with elapsed cooling time, growth and decay curves for each major induced element were summarized. A large amount of short-lived beta-decay radionuclides appeared while the accelerator was shut down; induced radionuclides with low activity were ignored due to low hazard. Considering the protection of radiation workers during maintenance or handling the equipment, research results show that lead (Pb) will produce the highest radiation effects when used as a coolant in a nuclear reactor, and it will require extra care as compared to water, gas, and other coolants included in this study.
                  </jats:p>
title: FLUKA-based assessment of induced radioactivity in iron target and surrounding coolants under 400 MeV carbon-ion irradiation
